notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 1 Chronicles 10, drawn from the approved source sites:

---

## OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

The Chronicler's account of Saul's death is an almost verbatim repetition of 1 Samuel 31. Dr. Constable notes that its purpose is to provide "a backdrop and a contrast for his portrayal of David" — Saul was "the king after the people's heart" (his name means "he who was requested"), while David was God's choice. The chapter also demonstrates the Chronicler's core theological theme: "blessing with faithfulness and judgment with disobedience." The writer recorded Saul's death at such length "to show that David had no hand in it." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-10.html)

Guzik likewise notes: "Having established Israel's historical setting and ethnic bounds in the preceding genealogies, the Chronicler now enters on his main subject, the history of the Hebrew kingdom, with its theological conclusions." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

Gaebelein adds that the writer of Chronicles uses Saul's departure to introduce "the history of the king after God's own heart, why God had dealt with Saul in judgment, and that the kingdom was turned unto David." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-10.html)

---

## VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — The Battle on Mount Gilboa

The Philistines fought against Israel, and Israel's men fled and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. Guzik explains that the Philistines had attacked deep into Israelite territory (1 Samuel 28:4), and Saul's army assembled at Gilboa. Because of "his deep rebellion against the LORD, Saul was not ready for battle: When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly (1 Samuel 28:5)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

The Pulpit Commentary provides geographical detail: Mount Gilboa is a mountain range about ten miles long, about six hundred feet high, in the territory of Issachar, flanked by the Little Hermon ridge to the north-east. The battle took place on the plains of Jezreel (Esdraelon). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/10.htm)

Poole, cited by Guzik, says: "Wonder not that Saul fell by the hands of the Philistines, who were armed against him by his own sin and by God's vengeance for it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

---

### v. 2 — Saul's Three Sons Killed

The Philistines pursued Saul and his sons closely, killing Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew verb for "followed hard after" implies the Philistines "made the pursuit of Saul and his sons their one special object." Luther's German is cited as "Hingen sich an Saul" — they clung to Saul. Abinadab is also called Ishui (1 Samuel 14:49). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/10.htm)

Precept Austin notes that three of Saul's four sons were killed; only Eshbaal ("man of Baal"), later renamed Ish-bosheth ("man of shame"), survived to become king after Saul. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

Guzik says of Jonathan: "The brave and worthy Jonathan died as he had lived – loyally fighting to the very end for his God, his country, and his father the king." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

---

### v. 3 — Saul Wounded by Archers

The battle grew heavy against Saul; archers found and wounded him. Precept Austin emphasises that this was no accidental hit: "The Philistine shot the arrow, but the LORD directed its course… In God's mind, it was Saul's time to step down from the monarchy." This connects directly to v. 14: "Therefore He (YAHWEH) killed him and turned the kingdom to David." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

Guzik quotes F.B. Meyer: "The flower of his army lay strewn around him; the chivalry of Israel was quenched in rivers of blood. Then, leaving all others, the Philistines concentrated their attack on that lordly figure which towered amid the fugitives, the royal crown on the helmet, the royal bracelet flashing on his arm." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

---

### v. 4 — Saul's Suicide

Saul, mortally wounded, asked his armour-bearer to kill him to avoid abuse by "these uncircumcised men." The armour-bearer refused out of fear, so Saul took his own sword and fell on it.

**On whether this was suicide:** Guzik follows Adam Clarke's reasoning that "He was to all appearance mortally wounded, when he begged his armourbearer to extinguish the remaining spark of life… though this wound accelerated his death, yet it could not be properly the cause of it, as he was mortally wounded before." However Guzik also states plainly that "God does regard suicide as sin; it is the sin of self-murder. Yet, we are wrong if we regard it as the unforgivable sin." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

G. Campbell Morgan (cited by both Guzik and Precept Austin) says: "Suicide is always the ultimate action of cowardice. In the case of Saul, and in many similar cases, it is perfectly natural; but let it never be glorified as heroic. It is the last resort of the man who dare not stand up to life." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

**On the armour-bearer's fear:** Precept Austin suggests he may have shared David's conviction that "one should not touch the LORD'S anointed," as evidenced by the fate of the Amalekite who claimed to have killed Saul (2 Samuel 1:14–16). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

**Precept Austin's spiritual note:** "Even to the end, Saul was focused on self. He was concerned with self-image. It is so sad that we see him cry out to his armor bearer but not cry out to Yahweh, Who Alone could save his soul from eternal punishment." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

---

### v. 5 — The Armour-Bearer's Suicide

Seeing Saul dead, the armour-bearer also fell on his sword and died. Precept Austin notes the text says Saul "was dead," not "appeared to be dead," which supports the conclusion that the Amalekite in 2 Samuel 1 was lying. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

Norman Geisler (cited on Precept Austin) lists Saul among five biblical suicides (with Abimelech, Zimri, Ahithophel, and Judas), noting "none of them is approved by God." He states: "Suicide is an attack on the image of God in man (Gen. 1:27) and an attempt to usurp God's sovereignty over human life." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

---

### v. 6 — "All His House Died Together"

"All his house" refers to those who went to war with Saul, not every family member. Precept Austin explains that Ish-bosheth survived (2 Samuel 2:8) and so did Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son (2 Samuel 4:4). Constable notes that the Chronicler "heightened the disastrous nature of Saul's death in subtle ways" compared to the 1 Samuel 31 account. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-10.html) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

---

### v. 7 — Israel's Panic and Flight

When the men of Israel in the valley saw the army had fled and Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities, and the Philistines occupied them. Guzik draws a parallel to Mark 14:27 — "I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" — and notes that Saul's sin and ruin "literally endangered the entire nation of Israel." The Philistine victory was so complete they cut Israel in half from west to east. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

---

### vv. 8–10 — Saul's Body Desecrated

The Philistines found Saul's body, stripped him, cut off his head, took his armour, and sent word throughout Philistia, proclaiming the news "in the temple of their idols." They put his armour in the temple of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.

Guzik notes two dimensions of disgrace: (1) in that culture, having your dead body treated this way "was considered a fate worse than death itself," and (2) "Saul's death was used to glorify pagan gods and to mock the living God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

The Ligonier devotional says: "Saul died as he lived, bringing shame on the name of the Lord… To them, Saul's defeat signified that Yahweh, the God of Israel, had lost in battle against the Philistine gods." The Philistines put Saul's armour in their "temple of Ashtaroth" (per 1 Samuel 31:8–10). (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saul-falls-to-philistines)

The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics observes the irony: the Philistines sent messengers "to carry tidings unto their idols" — informing their gods — which tacitly confesses the folly of idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/10.htm)

---

### vv. 11–12 — The Men of Jabesh-Gilead

All the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons, brought them to Jabesh, buried their bones under the oak (or tamarisk tree), and fasted seven days.

Guzik explains that these men acted out of gratitude: many years earlier Saul had delivered their city from the Ammonites (1 Samuel 11:1–11). David later thanked them (2 Samuel 2:4–7). Guzik adds: "In a time of disgrace, loss, and tragedy like this, God still has His valiant men to do His work." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

The Ligonier devotional notes: "Saul had a bad end, but as the Lord's anointed, he deserved a proper burial." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saul-falls-to-philistines)

Gaebelein describes their bravery: "the brave men of Jabesh-gilead marched all the weary night; they crossed Jordan; they climbed that steep brow, and silently detached the dead bodies from the walls." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-10.html)

---

### vv. 13–14 — The Theological Verdict: Why Saul Died

These two verses are unique to Chronicles — they do not appear in 1 Samuel 31. They are the Chronicler's own theological summary of Saul's downfall.

**Three reasons for Saul's death:**

1. **He did not keep the word of the LORD.** Gill specifies this refers to Saul's failure to wait for Samuel (1 Samuel 13:13) and his sparing of the Amalekites whom he was commanded to destroy (1 Samuel 15). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/10.htm)

2. **He consulted a medium for guidance** (the witch of Endor, 1 Samuel 28:7–14), which violated Leviticus 19:31. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/10.htm)

3. **He did not inquire of the LORD.** Ellicott notes that Saul did in fact inquire of the LORD before going to the medium (1 Samuel 28:6), but "the Lord answered him not, neither by the dreams, nor by the Urim, nor by the prophets." Ellicott explains: "Saul's natural impatience on this occasion betrayed him again; he at once despaired of help from his God, instead of seeking it with self-humiliation and penitence." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/10-14.htm)

Gill says Saul's inquiry was "in some sense in an external, careless, and hypocritical manner, yet not done seriously, sincerely, and heartily… it was accounted as if he inquired not at all." Poole, cited by Guzik, compares this to 1 Corinthians 11:20 — eating the Lord's supper in a sinful manner is accounted as not eating it at all. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

**"Therefore He killed him":** Ellicott explains that God acts through secondary means — "He employed the Philistines, and the suicidal hand of Saul himself; just as He employed the Assyrian conquerors… and raised up Cyrus to be His servant." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/10-14.htm)

Gill says "therefore he slew him; or suffered him to be slain." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/10.htm)

**"Turned the kingdom unto David":** This sentence shows the chapter is transitional to David's reign. Ellicott says the Chronicler's point is that "the sin that ruined the first king was essentially that which led to the final ruin of the nation, viz., unfaithfulness to the covenant-God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/10-14.htm)

---

## PROTESTANT TRADITIONAL DIFFERENCES

### Reformed / Ligonier

The Ligonier devotional (R.C. Sproul's ministry) emphasises God's sovereignty in Saul's death, seeing it as the culmination of "persistent, impenitent disobedience." It highlights the contrast with David: "The very same day, perhaps, that David was triumphing over the Amalekites, were the Philistines triumphing over Saul. One is set over against the other, that men may see what comes of trusting in God and what comes of forsaking him" (citing Matthew Henry). The lesson drawn is: "We cannot think that God will overlook disobedience in His servants. He is gracious, but He is willing to remove people from positions if they fail to serve Him." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saul-falls-to-philistines)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

Guzik's emphasis is practical and devotional: Saul "seeming to lack any genuine spiritual connection with God" was "easily and quickly corrupted by pride and fear." Suicide is treated as sin but not unforgivable — "Anyone who does commit suicide has given in to the lies and deceptions of Satan, whose purpose is to kill and destroy (John 10:10)." G. Campbell Morgan's statement that suicide is "the last resort of the man who dare not stand up to life" is given prominence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-10/)

### Gaebelein (Dispensational)

Gaebelein calls Saul's consultation of the medium "the agency of Satan, to a demon instrument for help and advice." He sees Saul's path as "the road of apostasy" and draws a parallel to "the apostasy in Christendom so prominent in the closing days of our age." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-chronicles-10.html)

### G. Campbell Morgan (Evangelical / Holiness)

Morgan's treatment is strongly moral: "Saul was a man than whom no other had greater opportunities, but his failure was disastrous… From the beginning he failed; step by step he declined in conduct and character, until he went out, dragging his nation into such confusion as threatened its very existence." He describes suicide as "the ultimate action of cowardice." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/1-chronicles-10.html) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

### Benson (Methodist / Wesleyan)

Benson notes the corporate consequences of royal sin: "Thus princes sin, and the people suffer for it. No doubt there was enough in them to deserve it. But that which divine justice had chiefly an eye to, was the sin of Saul. Great men should, in an especial manner, take heed of provoking God's wrath." On v. 14, Benson says Saul did inquire "but not in a right manner; not humbly and penitently, not diligently and importunately, not patiently and perseveringly; nor till he was brought to the last extremity, and then it was too late." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-chronicles-10.html)

---

## OTHER VIEWS

### Modern Scholarship (Dr. Constable, NET Bible notes direction)

Constable notes that the Chronicler heightened the disastrous nature of Saul's death compared to 1 Samuel 31:6–10 "in subtle ways" (citing Williamson and McConville). He also notes scholarly discussion about whether the Amalekite's account in 2 Samuel 1 was considered a fabrication even in ancient times. The Chronicler's presentation of Saul as "a foil meant to show the faithfulness of David" reflects standard scholarly understanding of the Chronicler's literary purpose. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-chronicles-10.html)

### On the Contradiction with 2 Samuel 1

Precept Austin dedicates substantial space to the question of who killed Saul — did he commit suicide (1 Samuel 31 / 1 Chronicles 10) or did the Amalekite kill him (2 Samuel 1)? Walter Kaiser concludes Saul did commit suicide and the Amalekite was lying to gain favour with David. Norman Geisler offers both harmonisation and contradiction views but leans toward the Amalekite's story being a fabrication. The Apologetics Study Bible proposes a three-wound complementary account: arrow wound, self-inflicted sword wound, and (possibly) the Amalekite's final blow. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-10-commentary)

### Catholic and Orthodox

No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter was located among the searched sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). Gill notes that the Targum (an ancient Jewish Aramaic paraphrase) "adds another reason of his death, because he killed the priests of Nob; but that is not in the text" — a point shared across traditions. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/10.htm)
